name: Gyroscope
plain: Reads how fast the device is rotating around three axes.
meaning: Shows how fast the device turns. Gyroscope noise has been used to eavesdrop on nearby speech (Gyrophone, 2014) and to fingerprint devices, which is why browsers cap the rate.

access.prompt_ui: Chromium shows no bubble: access follows the Motion sensors site setting (default Allow) plus the Permissions API name. Safari and Firefox do not ship the API.
access.persistence: Site setting Allow or Block per origin
access.iframe: Cross-origin iframes blocked unless allow="gyroscope"; page must be focused and visible
steps: 'reading' events fire; 'error' event on NotAllowedError or NotReadableError

data.metric: Sensor readings at the requested frequency

limits.headline: Can feel how fast your device turns while the page is open
limits.user_action: Nothing in most browsers. Chrome allows it by default unless you changed Motion sensors in site settings
can: Measure turning speed on three axes
Move a 3D view or game as you turn the phone
Help recognise your device through small sensor quirks
cannot: Run in Firefox or Safari, which do not support it
Run at full speed; browsers cap the rate to limit eavesdropping on speech
Show a prompt in Chrome; there is none by default
Measure turning while the page is closed
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet support it. Safari and Firefox do not.

story.what_it_is: The page reads how fast your device is turning.

marketing.name: Generic Sensor API
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes a common way for web pages to read motion and environment sensors such as accelerometer and gyroscope.

story.for_you: You twist your phone and a game camera turns, or a 360 photo spins. On many phones there is no big prompt. The sensor can also pick up tiny sounds from nearby speech.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for smooth camera control in 3D and AR. Trackers can use sensor quirks to recognize a phone, and research showed it can eavesdrop on speech nearby.

use_cases.example: A browser first person game or 3D viewer turns the camera as you turn your phone.
A web AR try on page uses turning speed to keep models fixed in place.
A 360 degree video pans smoothly as you twist your phone.
A web map turns as you turn, with smooth compass behavior.
Researchers showed a page could pick up speech through gyroscope vibration, an eavesdropping risk.
A fingerprinting script uses tiny gyro errors to recognize one phone among millions.

technical_bounds: 60 Hz cap mitigates the audio side channel

history.change: Gyrophone shows speech recovery from gyroscope sampled near 200 Hz
